newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge restores securities suit vs Philip Morris.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge restores securities suit vs Philip Morris.

text.p: A federal judge on Wednesday reinstated a class-action shareholder suit against Philip Morris Cos. Inc. that claims the company hid negative information about smoking from investors.

U.S. District Judge Michael Mukasey said he restored the suit because of the recent emergence of documents that present new evidence of alleged misrepresentations and omissions by the tobacco company.

In the lawsuit, which names Philip Morris and four company executives as defendants, the plaintiffs said the company artifically inflated the stock price by maintaining the public stance "that nicotine is not addictive (and) that smoking is entirely a matter of 'choice.'"
Mukasey had dismissed the original complaint in September 1995, saying that "Philip Morris's statements were permissible statements of opinion."

In his latest opinion, the judge cited newly discovered evidence that specifically identified Philip Morris and tobacco industry documents discussing studies concerning whether cigarettes and nicotine are addictive.

"This new documentary evidence is of enough potential importance and volume that I probably would not have granted defendants' motion to dismiss had it been described in the initial complaint," Mukasey said, adding, "Most of this evidence is admissible."

In a written statement, Philip Morris said "Yesterday's decision by a federal judge to permit plaintiffs to proceed with an amended complaint alleging violations of federal securities laws is not a ruling on the merits of the plaintiffs' claims. Philip Morris believes the allegations in the complaint have little or no legal support and ultimately the claims should be dismissed."
For Philip Morris, the world's largest cigarette maker with its Marlboro, Virginia Slims and Merit brands, the suit is yet another courtroom attack in an already crowded field.

The company, along with the rest of the industry, is defending class-action suits from more than 20 state attorneys general who are trying to recoup state healthcare funds spent treating smoking-related illnesses.

Alongside the state suits are several separate personal-injury suits, a state-by-state collection of private class-action suits, and the onset of regulation by the Food and Drug Administration, something tobacco companies have never faced before.

The judge said the evidence submitted in the shareholder suit identifies Philip Morris as "discussing the manipulation of nicotine levels in cigarettes, sworn statements from three former Philip Morris researchers ... discussing the companies alleged knowledge" of nicotine addictiveness, and recent government actions declaring nicotine as an addictive drug.

The suit was brought by shareholders who bought Philip Morris stock between roughly 1993 and 1994, according to plaintiffs' attorney Dan Krasner of New York law firm Wolf Haldenstein Adler Freeman & Herz.

"If Philip Morris had available to it not one but several studies tending to show that nicotine was addictive, and if the company manipulated nicotine levels in order to take advantage of that perceived addictive quality, such evidence could show that, contrary to its public statements, the company was aware of undisclosed facts tending to show that its products were subject to FDA regulation or other restriction," the judge wrote in his order.
"The judge concludes (the documents) clearly indicate that Philip Morris was on notice about the addictive effects of nicotine from its own internal studies," Krasner said.
Krasner said he also expects to seek access to the documents recently turned over by Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group Inc. to the state attorneys general.

Those documents, purported to contain evidence the company knew nicotine was addictive and that cigarettes cause cancer, were released as a condition of Liggett's settlement of the state Medicaid suits and a handful of private personal-injury suits.

"It was certainly out of the blue," said Roy Burry, tobacco analyst at Oppenheimer & Co., said of the shareholder suit. Burry said that even though the suit seems to add to the industry's woes, the suit could prove problematic for the plaintiffs.

"It would seem to me to be more difficult (than personal injury-based suits) to prove, because you have to prove securities violation along with all the (personal injury) stuff that all the other guys are trying to prove," Burry said.
